sections.label: 01 / ESTABLISHED RESEARCH
sections.title: Quantum Geometry
sections.question: Can the quantum geometry of noninteracting bands guide our understanding of correlated matter?
sections.text: Quantum geometry encodes how Bloch wave functions vary with momentum. For time-reversal-breaking Chern bands, Kähler geometry provides a framework for understanding ideal band geometry and its connection to fractional Chern insulators. Our work generalizes this geometric language to time-reversal-symmetric Kramers pairs: quaternion-Kähler structures and non-Abelian metric–curvature relations offer a starting point for asking analogous questions in systems that preserve time reversal.
sections.note: This framework provides a starting point for identifying geometric conditions relevant to time-reversal-symmetric correlated phases.

sections.label: 02 / ESTABLISHED RESEARCH
sections.title: Band Topology
sections.question: What topological information is lost when we look only at the occupied bands?
sections.text: Some band-topological structures depend on the wave functions of both occupied and unoccupied states. In the real Hopf insulator, we characterized delicate three-dimensional topology in four-band systems with spinless PT symmetry, including independent Hopf invariants and associated boundary phenomena. I am also interested in the structure of unconventional topological phase transitions.
sections.note: These results highlight why the full multiband wave-function structure matters for topological classification.

sections.label: 03 / BROADER RESEARCH INTERESTS
sections.title: Correlated Quantum Matter
sections.question: How do the traces of noninteracting band structure shape what emerges from electron correlations?
sections.text: My broader interests include correlations in electronic bands, topological order, symmetry-protected topological phases, and generalized symmetries. I hope to investigate how multiband quantum geometry can constrain or guide the emergence of time-reversal-symmetric correlated phases.
sections.note: A future direction is to connect single-particle geometric constraints with concrete many-body models and observables.
